Who sits in the chair down here?

scenes.text: You again. Good. I had half a sentence saved for you and I've lost it. Ask.

buttons.name: What did the truce really say?
Who sits in the chair down here?

scenes.text: Speak low. I am borrowing this breath from a tune and it will be wanted back.

buttons.name: What did the truce really say?
Who sits in the chair down here?

scenes.text:
Three lines. I can still see his breath in the lamp.

They take back the army they called. Every third night is theirs: no bell is rung, they walk above as guests, and any of ours who wish may walk below. And it is sworn on their crown, not his, which he may not wear and they would not touch.

That's all. No souls. No firstborn. No trick. Everything that went wrong after went wrong on our side of the paper.

He was the only man at court who never laughed at me. Do you know how rare that is, for a king? They're raised to it.

He took their pledge in his bare right hand because it was offered to him, and it would have been rude to ask for a cloth. It bit him to the bone. He never used that hand again and he never once mentioned it.

At my trial I had one defence. "I remember him." It was true and it was sufficient and they burned me for it.

"Someone must." Yes. I ran out of candle. They came for me before I could find another.

You'll have imagined something grand. Someone must wear the crown. Someone must slay the thing.

It was: someone must go down and say good morning. That's the whole discovery. Thirty years, a hundred bells, and that's all of it. They had been knocking for four hundred years and nobody had answered the door.

A thing sworn can be sworn again. But only by someone who's first bothered to say hello.

...

Well.

That's the first time anyone's said it to me, as it happens. In either world.

Get out before I become sentimental. It puts me off the note.

Magda? The small one? She's ALIVE?

She was twelve. She carried the ninth notebook into a swamp in the dark with hounds behind her, and I never knew if...

Tell her this, exactly. Tell her she still holds a pen like a trowel. She'll know it's me. Nobody else was ever that rude to her.

No.

Not from me. I'll teach you every art there is and I'll tell you what was said at that table to the word. But who sits there is a thing you'll want to have worked out yourself, standing up, before you see him. It will matter to you that you did. It will matter to him.

You have all the pieces. Three people up there are each holding one. Go and be a nuisance to an archivist.

He's stopped.

I felt it go out of the note like a string cut. The whole Choir went a hair sharp. They don't know what to do without him. Neither do I, as it happens.

I held the lamp for him once, at the table. I should have liked to hold it at the end. I gather you did that instead, in your fashion. Was he...

No. Don't tell me. I remember him. That was always the point of me.

Of course he did. The red one. He used to read it on the walls on the third nights, when he thought no one could see.

The chair's empty now, and it wants someone who can hear all of this at once and not break. If that's to be you, then listen to an old flat voice: keep the truce. It was a good one. It was only ever kept by one man.

Mind the edge. People come up the cliff stair looking at the view and go down it a lot faster.

Kesh Cinder. Wingmistress, which means I teach. I don't fly. Mine was shot down two summers ago over the Saltglass, and they don't get up from that.

You're reading the wall. Everyone does.

The Cinder Roost. Ysolt Cinder cut the first ledge with a borrowed pick. She walked into the Saltglass with a dead mule and came out a year later on something with wings. She never said what she promised.

When the grey army came down from the north, this was the one province it never held. Nothing that marches in step crosses open sand under dragons. We've kept riders since, the way other places keep walls.

The roll. Every rider the Roost has lost, and their dragon beside them, because they go together more often than not.

I read it out loud on the first morning of every season. All of it. It takes most of an hour. The cadets fidget for the first half and stop fidgeting for the second.

Mine is on there. Her name, not mine. I'm still down here being useful.

buttons.name: How do I become a rider?

scenes.text: Don't be. Be careful. It's more use to me.

Everyone wants to ride. Half of them want to be seen riding, which is different and gets you killed faster.

Three things. You cross the Span: a stone bridge over the gorge, one block wide, older than the town, and it doesn't hold together everywhere. Then the Choosing: you walk into the nesting field and the dragons decide what they think of you. Then you keep an egg warm until it hatches, and if it hatches for you, you're theirs.

Fall off the Span and you wait for next season. Walk into the field like a fool and you'll be burned for it.

Then I read your name out next season with the others, and somebody fidgets through it.

That's not me being hard. That's the Roost. Nobody here was ever told it was safe, so nobody here was ever lied to.

Then you're a cadet. Congratulations. It means nothing yet.

The Span is past the gate. Walk it end to end. Don't stop in the middle to admire anything. Some of the stones crumble when you stand on them, and the wind comes up the gorge in gusts. Lean into it.

Come back when you're across. Or don't, and I'll know which.
Cadet. You haven't crossed yet.
Still on this side of the gorge, I see. The Span hasn't moved.
The wind's from the east today. Lean left.
You're welcome to stand here. The Span isn't going to cross itself.

Don't look down, everyone says. Wrong. Look down a little, at your feet, at the next stone. Look at the gate when you're nearly there.

And if one goes under you, don't stop. Stopping is what kills people. The next one's usually fine.

Across. Good. You looked at the gate, I saw.

Now the nesting field. Here is the whole of my advice, and I'm only going to say it once. Put your weapon away. Don't run. Walk up to a nest slowly, with your hands empty, and let it look at you.

They can smell fear and they can smell a blade, and they don't like either. Do it right and one of them will let you take an egg.

buttons.name: And if they don't like me?

scenes.text:
Then you'll be on fire, and they won't look at you again until tomorrow.

People have tried sneaking in with a sword behind their back. A dragon doesn't care which hand it's in.
It let you take one. Now set it on a Roost in your own keep and wait.
Is it warm? Keep it warm.
Don't hover over it. Eggs know when they're being watched.
You keep looking at the sky. It won't hatch faster for that.

One thing. On the third night, at seventeen past three, it will go cold and quiet as a stone, and you'll think it's dead.

It isn't. They all do it. Every dragon in the Waste does something at that hour. Stay with it. Don't leave it alone that night.

No, I won't tell you why. Ask me again when you've earned it.

It hatched for you. I heard.

Then it's done. The dragon's half and yours. Go to a Tree of Oaths and swear it. Say it out loud. They like that.

And come back. I teach riders too, not only cadets.
Rider. What do you need?

buttons.name: Why won't they fly on the third night?

scenes.text: Rider. Your name's still off the roll. Let's keep it that way.

buttons.name: Why won't they fly on the third night?

scenes.text: There's sand in your hair. Good. You've been up.

buttons.name: Why won't they fly on the third night?

scenes.text: She's watching us from the ledge, you know. Wave.

buttons.name: Why won't they fly on the third night?

scenes.text:
Salt-carrier's daughter. Nobody special, which she'd want you to know. Her mule died a day into the Saltglass and she kept walking, because going back was further.

She used to say you don't tame one, you're introduced. She never said who did the introducing.

That's an elder's question, and the elders will tell you it's the moon, or the heat, or that dragons are lazy on a third night like everyone else.

They're lying. I'll tell you that much for free.

The rest, when you're a Drake-Captain. Not before. It's not a thing you carry easily.

Fly high when you're looking and low when you're running. Raider camps show from above: smoke in the day, fires at night, and a trampled ring where they drill.

And land before she's tired, not when. She'll fly till her heart breaks if you let her. Don't let her.

You're sworn to something already. I can see it on you.

The Roost doesn't take halves. One road each, that's the rule everywhere I know of, and the dragons keep it stricter than we do.

You can still look at the wall, if you want. Everyone does.
The first. A salt-carrier's daughter with a dead mule. She never said what she promised, only that the dragon set the terms.

She takes the board down off its hooks and holds it so the light falls across it. She doesn't need to. She knows every name.

She reads them anyway, all of them, at the same pace, and doesn't skip her own dragon's.

Drake-Captain. Then sit, and I'll give you what I promised.

This is Ysolt's last page. The elders have a copy and say it was written in fever. It wasn't.

"The night the grey army went, every dragon in the Waste came down at once. Not at dusk. At seventeen past three. They folded their wings and put their heads under them like birds in a storm, and the sky over the north went the wrong colour, and something up there was eating an army. Nobody else looked up. I did. I will not fly on that night again, and neither will she."

That's the word she used. The songs say the grey army died of cold in a pass. Ysolt says it was taken, all of it, in one breath, by something that doesn't live under our sky.

The elders know. They've known for three hundred years. They teach cadets that dragons are lazy on a third night, because the truth is worse for recruiting.

Now you know too. Don't tell the cadets. Tell them when they're you.

Dragonlord.

Your name's going on the wall. The other wall, where Ysolt's is: the ones who lived long enough to matter. I carved it last night. It's crooked. I was crying, a bit, and you'll never prove it.

When the bad night comes, and it's coming, you'll be in the air over the Rift with fire in your hands. That's what a Dragonlord is for. Not the sky. The ground under it.

And one more thing, since you've earned it. You know they won't fly at seventeen past three on a siege night. The elders say "never". It isn't never. Once in a Dragonlord's life, she'll fly through it for you, if you ask her at that hour. Once. Ysolt did. She said you can see the whole host from up there, waiting in the dark.

They're saying the knocking has stopped.

I've a favour to ask, and I've never asked a rider for anything. Take me up. Just once. Behind you. I won't hold on, I'll just sit, and I won't say anything, and you won't look round.

...Thank you. She'd have liked you.
Something you wanted?
Back again. The view hasn't changed.
You're the one who reads the wall. Hello.
Mind the edge. I said that last time too.

Shut the door. You're letting the cold at her.

...There. You can hear her settle. Four hundred years she's been burning, and she still sulks at a draught.

Ulla. I keep the fire. You'll want to warm your hands. Everybody does. Go on.

Hroda Deepforge. Bellfounder. She lit it under the mountain and swore it would outlast her, and she wasn't a woman who swore lightly.

When the grey army came down and cut the bells off every tower in the north, every new bell was poured here. Forty nights at Rimehold taught us that a wall is only as good as what it's bound with.

They were rung. Some of them were rung till they cracked.

Afterwards the grey brothers came north, very polite, and took the moulds away for safekeeping. I've never known what they were keeping them safe from.

They couldn't carry off the fire, though. They tried. Ask me about the three brothers who tried, one day, when I've had a drink.

Help. Hm.

There's a side-hearth gone cold this thirty years, since my brother's hands went. I could light it, if somebody hauled for it. Sixteen iron and sixteen coal, and not the rubbish from the surface seams.

If you mean it, haul. If you don't, there's the door. Shut it behind you.

Honest question. Honest answer: probably nothing. Most who haul for me go home with sore arms and a story.

Now and then the fire takes to somebody. Then it's something else. I don't decide that. She does.

Good. Sixteen iron ingots, sixteen coal. Bring them here and I'll take them off you when you're standing in front of me.

I don't take promises. I take iron.
Sixteen iron ingots and sixteen coal. I'll take them when you have them on you.
Iron? Coal? No? Then why are you letting the cold in?
Sixteen and sixteen. I'm not going to forget the number.
She's sulking. She knows the side-hearth's waiting.

That's Hroda's hand-bell pattern. First one poured in thirty years, and it came out sweet.

Take it to the lake at Rimehold. Set it down on the ice at night and ring it. Something out there still answers bells.
You've still got the bell. I can hear it in your pack, humming.
The lake. At night. On the ice. I said all three.
Don't ring it in here. She'll never forgive either of us.

The Rimehold folk call it the Huntsman. It wears a knight's cloak and runs hounds across the ice, and it went under after somebody a long time ago.

It comes up for bells. All the old things do. That's why the grey army cut them.

Bring it down, and come back.
He's up. Now he has to go back down.
You rang it. I felt the lake take the note, all the way up here.
He's up, then. Go and put him down.
There's frost on you. Lake frost. You've been close.

So he's down.

Hroda used to say a smith never made a weapon she was proud of, or a bell she was ashamed of. You took a bell out to the ice and did with it what a bell's for. That's smith's work.

The fire's taken to you. I can see it. Go to a Tree of Oaths and swear. Then come back, and I'll start teaching you properly.
What do you need?
Smith. Shut the door. Good. You're learning.
She brightened when you came in. Don't let it go to your head.
Your hands have changed. They hold a hammer like it belongs to them now.

Steel remembers. Quench it angry and it stays angry. Quench it in a hurry and it never quite settles.

When you gear your guards, do it slow, and do it yourself. They stand straighter in steel that was made for them, and they know.

South. The grey brothers' chapterhouse, I'd guess, in a cellar with a lock on it.

One of those moulds is half of something that matters. That's all I'll say until you're a Master Smith. A thing like that, you don't go after on your first winter.

She had arms like a bridge and a voice like one too. Her apprentices were all afraid of her, and all of them named a daughter after her.

Three generations after her, the biggest bell this land ever had was poured right where you're standing. She'd have hated how it was used. She'd have loved how it rang.

You're sworn already. I can see it on you. She can too: look, she's gone quiet.

One road each. Warm your hands, though. Nobody's turned away from the fire.

Master Smith. Sit by her. She likes you now; you can tell by how she ticks.

The moulds. The grey brothers took every bell mould in the north and said it was to keep them safe. One of them was half of the biggest bell this land ever poured. Three generations after Hroda, right here, they cast a bell so big it took the whole mountain's fire for a week.

They rang it at Bellhollow, once, at the end of the war. It split. And whatever it rang out, it stayed out.

My grandmother said: the same thing the first bell rang out, when there was a queen and the country had another name. Bells don't keep out cold or wolves. They never did. Every bell in the north was made to keep something on the far side of a door.

That's why the grey army cut them. That's why the brothers hid the moulds instead of melting them. You don't melt a key you might need.

Forgemaster. She knows your name. I heard her say it.

I wrote to the chapterhouse. Brother Cael sent the mould back on a cart with no guard and a note: "It was never ours to keep." Make of that what you like. I've made a tongue from it.

One stroke. That's all it has in it, each time. When the dead stand up in rows, ring it, and they'll remember they were never soldiers. Hroda would have been proud of it. It isn't a weapon.

Shut the door.

...No. Leave it open. Let her feel the air.

Four hundred years she's burned without stopping, in case. I'm going to let her down to embers tonight and sleep in the chair. If she goes out, she goes out. I don't think she will. I think she's tired, the same as me.
Well?
Door. Shut. Thank you.
Back for the warmth? Everyone comes back for the warmth.
She's in a good mood today. Must be the coal.

Name? No, don't tell me yet. Let me look first.

...No. You're not in it. Good, or a pity, depending.

Ottilie Holt, harbourmistress. This is the Debt Book. Everybody who's ever captained out of Gull's Rest is in it, and what they owe, and who to.

Holt's Debt. Merrin Holt, my ancestor, burned forty Saltreach boats in the harbour mouth so the grey army's second fleet couldn't land. The crews agreed. The owners weren't asked.

We've been paying for those boats ever since. Every captain signs the articles and takes a share. That's why a Saltreach crew obeys: they know exactly what their captain owes, and to whom.

Never once marked paid. Three hundred years of money in, and the book still says what it said.

I used to think that was greed. Some clerk's trick. I've stopped thinking that. I don't know what I think now.

Always. The sea takes them faster than the town makes them.

Three things. You sign the articles and pay your first share of the debt. You raise a crew, three hands at least, sworn to your keep. And you do one thing that tells the sea who you are.

There's a woman in a wedding dress at the sunken chapel. She's been waiting at that altar since before the book was opened. Somebody needs to lay her to rest.

buttons.name: Why does the sea need telling?

scenes.text: Because a captain is somebody the sea has agreed to blame. It wants to know your name before it starts.

Read them later. Everybody does, and everybody wishes they'd read them first.

Your share is thirty-two Regals. Pay it to me when you've got it on you, and your name goes in the book below mine.
Thirty-two Regals for your share. I'll take it when you have it on you.
Thirty-two Regals. The book's open. The pen's wet.
Your line in the book is still blank. It's waiting.
Debt doesn't go away for being ignored. I'd know.
You're in the book. Now raise a crew: three guards sworn to your keep, and tell me when you have them.
No crew yet? A captain alone is a passenger with opinions.
Three hands, sworn to your keep. Then come and tell me.
You'll want ones who can swim. Not everyone thinks to ask.
You have a crew. Now take them to the sunken chapel. The Bride is waiting.
Three hands. It's a crew if you say it loudly enough.
The chapel tower shows above the water when the moon's dark. That's your night.
She's still waiting. Somebody ought to stop her.

Nothing she'll want to hear. She's been waiting for a groom who isn't coming, and part of her knows.

Be quick and be kind. Those aren't always different things.

You laid her down. I heard it from the lighthouse: the lamp flickered, first time in my life.

Then you're a captain in all but the oath. Go to a Tree of Oaths and swear it. Your share of the debt goes up, and so does what they'll do for you.
What do you need, Captain?

buttons.name: Can I read the whole book?

scenes.text: Captain. Your share's paid up this season. Mine isn't. Don't tell anyone.

buttons.name: Can I read the whole book?

scenes.text: Your crew drink in the Gull. They speak well of you. Mostly.

buttons.name: Can I read the whole book?

scenes.text: The book's open. It's always open. Sit.

buttons.name: Can I read the whole book?

scenes.text:
She lit the first boat herself. Then she stood on the quay all night and watched the other thirty-nine catch. She didn't sleep for three days after.

The crews went home. That's the part nobody tells. They agreed to it, and they went home, and then later... well. Later is in the book.

Not yet. When you're Captain in rank as well as name.

There are names in the back that I have to read to people myself, in a quiet room. You'll understand why.

Your crew fight for the share of the debt you carry so they don't have to. Carry it well.

And never let one of them drown before you. No Saltreach crew ever has. It would leave them holding the debt.

You're sworn already. I can see it. The book can't take you twice and neither can the sea.

You can still read the front pages, if you like. They're the pretty ones.
Forty boats, burned in the harbour mouth by Merrin Holt, my ancestor, to stop a fleet. Three hundred years of paying for them, and the book still says unpaid.

Captain in rank. Then come into the back room and shut the door.

The back of the book. The forty crews of the forty boats, every name, in Merrin's own hand. They went home after the burning. They lived. And then, over the years, on third nights, they started walking into the water. One here, a family there. Merrin wrote each one in as it happened.

Nobody knows. The town calls those years the Lost Days and doesn't talk about them. But here's what I worked out, alone in this room, last winter.

The debt's never been marked paid because it isn't owed to the boat owners. It's owed to the crews. And you can't pay someone who's dead. You can only pay someone who isn't.

I think they're somewhere. I think the lamp at the lighthouse hasn't gone out in three hundred years because somebody is still at sea.

Don't repeat that in the Gull. They'll take my chain off.

Admiral. Merrin never had that word.

I want you to do something I can't. When you go under, wherever the bad road takes you, look for them. There's water under everything, the old songs say, and it runs. Forty crews of Saltreach are rowing somewhere, still owed.

Find them. Settle with them. Tell them a Holt sent you, and that the book is open. If they'll take one more stroke for a captain, it'll be for you.

Sit. Watch.

She opens the Debt Book to the first page, dips the pen, and in a careful hand under Merrin Holt's name she writes one word. Then she blots it, and sits back, and looks at it for a long time.

"Paid." The first time anyone has. Out at the lighthouse, the lamp is going out.
What can I do for you?
Back. Still not in the book.
The tide's on the turn. You've got a minute.
Ink, rope or gossip? I've got all three.

Mind the plank, it's thinking about sinking. Come in, come in. Kettle's on. Kettle's always on.

Nell Sedge. You'll have heard of Goody Sedge. Everyone in the fen has. She's my great-great-something, and three villages each show you her grave, and one of them is keeping a spot warm for me.

Sit. Tea first. Then you can ask.

buttons.name: Thank you. What is this place?

scenes.text:
Home. It floats, mostly. When the water's high I'm further out and when it's low I'm in the mud with the eels, and either way nobody from the Order wants to walk to me. Which is the point.

They came once, years before my time, to burn books. There weren't any. There never are. What a witch knows is handed over in a cup.

Magda. Yes. We haven't spoken in sixty years, and I'm sure she'd tell you whose fault that is.

She borrows from something old and won't say what. The fen lends too, mind you. It just tells you the interest up front. That's the difference, and it's the whole difference.

Keeps children alive through a wet summer, mostly. Finds lost things. Tells you which of your neighbours is standing a little wrong. Puts down what needs putting down.

It isn't a gift. The fen doesn't give. It lends. And when it wants paying, it wants it all at once.

Would you like to learn? I'm not asking lightly.

A night, to start. You drink, and the fen takes a little something to know you by. You'll feel heavy and you won't see well, and in the morning you'll be fine.

After that, it asks when it asks. I've never been asked for anything I couldn't pay. I know people who have.

Then here's the cup. No, don't look in it. Nobody ever looks in it.

You can drink it now, or go away and think and drink it later. The tea will keep. It's very patient tea.
Your cup's waiting.
The cup's still here. So are you. One of you is going to have to make a move.
Come back for your tea? It's kept. I said it would.
Sit. The cup's on the side. Whenever you like.

There. That's the first payment.

You'll feel it in a moment. Sit down before you do. The fen's having a look at you. Let it.

When you can stand again, go and find Goody Sedge's graves. All three. Kneel at each, and leave her something. One of them will give you something back, and then you'll know she's had a look at you too.
Have you knelt at all three?
Three graves. Three villages. She got about, Goody.
Kneel. Leave something. Don't be fussy about what.
Feeling better? It passes. Mostly.

In three villages of the fen, and each one swears theirs is the real one. Look in the oldest corner of the burying ground, under the willow, where the stone's gone soft.

They're all real. That's the joke nobody gets.
Goody Sedge has had her look. Now the fen wants one thing done.
She gave you something back. I knew she would. She always liked the polite ones.
The Mother of Changelings. Have you been to see her yet?
The fen's waiting on you. It isn't patient like the tea.

There's a thing in the fen that takes children and leaves something else in the cot. The Mother of Changelings, they call her, and she's older than any of my grandmothers.

The fen has been owed her for a very long time. End her, and come back for tea.

She's gone. I felt it in the water, like a stone settling.

Then the fen knows you, and Goody knows you, and I suppose I know you too. Go to a Tree of Oaths and swear it. Say it nicely.

And come back. There's more in the cup than a first lesson.
What do you need?

buttons.name: How do I see who's wrong?

scenes.text: Witch. Sit, the kettle's on. It's always on.

buttons.name: How do I see who's wrong?

scenes.text: You've got that look. The fen's been talking to you. Tell me.

buttons.name: How do I see who's wrong?

scenes.text: Mind the plank. Oh, you did. Good.

buttons.name: How do I see who's wrong?

scenes.text:
The fen never takes one of anything. If you hurt one, hurt the one in the middle, and let it spread.

And always leave something when you take something. A ribbon, a crust, a song. It isn't superstition. It's book-keeping.

Nobody knows when she lived. Before Aldmere had a name, I'd say, and before anyone thought to disapprove of her.

She kept a list of everyone the fen lent to, and what they paid. It was never written down. It was handed over in a cup, like everything else. I've got it. One day you will.

Watch the ones who face the wrong way when nobody's looking, and the dogs who won't go near them.

When you're further along, the fen will show you plainer. Be kind about what you see. Most of them never asked to come back the way they did.

Oh, you're sworn already. I can taste it on the air. The fen won't lend to someone who owes elsewhere. It's very particular about that.

Have some tea anyway. Tea's free. Tea's the only thing that is.

Crone. Come on, then. Bring the lantern. No, the other one.

She poles the raft out past where the reeds stop, to a patch of water so still it looks like a hole. The ground around it is wrong: half of it is fen, and half of it is something else, darker, like a stone that's been under water too long and forgot it was ever dry.

"This is the old water. This is where the fen does its lending from."

For something older than Aldmere. This land had another name once, when two kinds of ground lay together here and neither minded. The fen still calls the place by that name. I won't say it out in the open, and you shouldn't either, not until you have to.

That's who the fen lends for. Something that used to live here, and was put out, and has been knocking ever since. Goody Sedge knew. Now you do.

Because Magda borrows from it and won't say so, and the Order pretends it never was, and somebody ought to know the truth without being frightened of it.

Be kind to it, when you meet it. It isn't wicked. It's owed.

Fen Mother.

Goody Sedge has a fourth grave now. I dug it myself, under the willow. It's got your name on, kept warm. That's the best compliment a Sedge can pay, so don't make that face.

When the bad night comes, the fen will call in everything it's lent at once. You'll feel it. Let it through you. And when you're falling, it'll lend you one more moment. Take it.

She's already got her coat on.

"I'm going to Magda's. Don't look like that. Sixty years is long enough to be right about something."

She poles away into the reeds with two cups and the kettle, and you hear, a long while later and a long way off, two old women not saying anything to each other for an hour.
What can I do for you?
Back! Sit. Kettle's on.
The plank held. It's fond of you.
You again. Good. I was running out of people to talk to who aren't eels.

You're dripping light. Everyone from the bright side does, for a while. It wears off.

I saw the crack open from the cart road. I thought someone ought to come and look, and nobody else would, so here I am, sitting on a dock, talking to it.

Have you come to take the cart's place? He said someone would, one day.

The ore cart. I drive it. Every dawn, from the villages, down the long rail to the south end, to the Seat. I bring it back empty.

What goes in it is Choir Ore. What it is for, you'd better see for yourself. Go to Glimwade, up the bank on the left. Watch them load it. I'll meet you there.

Him in the Chair. Morvane.

Don't look like that. Everyone up there knows the name, I'm told. You shout it at your walls on the third night.

I've driven past him a hundred times. I have never once seen his face. You don't look up when you pass the Chair. That's the first thing you learn.

The Carter. That's what I do, so that's what I'm called.

We don't have names down here, not the way you do. A name is something you give to someone who has lost theirs. Nobody's ever lost mine. I never had one to lose.

Is it? You lot have names and you still forget each other.

Go to Glimwade. Up the bank on the left, where the lamps are. Watch the cart. Then come and find me.
Glimwade. Up the bank on the left, where the lamps are. Watch them load the cart, and then we'll talk. I'll be there before you.
Ask what you like. If I don't know, I'll say. If I do know and I'm frightened to say it, I'll say that too.
You came back. People from the bright side mostly don't. Ask.
Keep your voice down near the rails. They carry.
The cart's out. I've got till it comes back. Ask me something.

It sings. Hit it and it holds the note. That's the whole of it.

Every stone goes south to the Seat, and from the Seat to the Court, and the Singers in the Court hold it while they sing. They sing at the Door. The Door gets wider.

Every night your walls get knocked on, somebody down here dug for it.

Morvane. That's all I've got. He hums your songs sometimes, ones nobody down here knows. That's how we know he's one of yours.

He never looks at the river. Everyone looks at the river; it's the only light we have. He looks up. Like a man waiting for a bell.

Small. Loud. Cracked voice, like a gate. They took him from Highcut to sing in the Court because you could hear him three seams away.

That's what the Court is. Ours. Our little ones, mostly, the loud ones. Whatever you've been told up there, the Choir is just us, singing because we were told to.

West of the Cross, the old hall where two kings sat down. East, past Cartmeet, the Standing Ranks. Far west, the Door. The stones east of the path that forgot to fall: climb to the top one. And the Seams, past Cartmeet, where the rail starts.

See three of them and come back. Then you'll know enough to see the Court.

The table's still there? Both chairs?

One knocked over. Yes. Ours stayed sitting. My grandmother said the one who knocked his over was the one who ran, and the one who stayed was the one who meant it.

She never said which side was which. I always assumed.

We were told they were a gift. An army, all of it, given to us to keep, because your king asked us to take it away.

An empty place at the front? That'll be the one who leads them. The one with the splinter in his head. We gave him back. Morvane wanted him.

It's the only door we had. Your side shut it with a bell, and the bell broke doing it, and the crack's the bell's.

My mother dug there. Her mother dug there. You wouldn't call it a war, what we're doing. It's knocking. For three hundred years. On our own front door.

You saw him lift his hand? The left one?

He always does it with the left. The right one he keeps in his lap. My father said it was hurt a long time ago, before he came down, and it never healed, because nothing up there heals down here.

That was you? On the trestle?

The cart didn't come back this morning. I walked the rail and found it in the river, and I stood there and I laughed, and then I was sick, and then I laughed again.

He'll know someone did it. He won't know who. Neither will I, if anyone asks.

The Highcut lot told me. You wouldn't let them risk it.

They talk about you now. That's not nothing, down here. Nobody talks about anybody. Go to any Tally once he's gone and see if they don't treat you right.
Not far yet. Go and look at something. I'll be here. I'm always here, or on the rail.

You've seen enough. I can tell. You've got the look we get after our first cart.

The Court gate opens to one note, for the cart, every dawn. I've hummed it a thousand times. Listen. Then do it back to me. Lower. Lower than that. There.

That's the Cartsong. The gate will take you for a cart. It won't know the difference till you're inside.

The singer with the cracked voice is my brother. When they fall quiet in there, they don't die. They just stop. Bring him out to me, if you can. I'll be at the Court door.

Still here. I'll be here until it's done, one way or the other.

You hum it at the gate. Don't hurry it. If the Court hears a cart in a hurry, it knows.

They came out. All of them. Holding their throats, walking past me like they were going home from a shift.

He came out. Not a sound left in him. He knew me, though. He put his hand on my face like he used to.

I'd like you to do something for me. Give me a name. That's what you do for someone who's lost theirs, and I think I've lost the Carter. There's no more cart.

Lark.

That's a bird, isn't it? One of yours, up in the light. Loud. Sings when it isn't told to.

Yes. I'll have that.

Morrow.

Tomorrow. The day after the one you're in. We don't have those down here, not really. Every day is the cart.

Yes. I'll have that.

Dawn.

The cart went at dawn. Every day of my life. Now it's just going to be a time of day.

Yes. I'll have that.

Now you go south. Up the long climb to the Seat.

He was given a name too, you know. The one in the Chair. Somebody down here gave it to him when he came, because he'd lost his own. Nobody alive remembers what it was before.

He's never once looked at the river. Go and see what he's looking up at.
The Court's quiet. You can hear the river now. I never knew it made a noise.
Say it again. My name. I like hearing it.
The rail's quiet. I keep waking at dawn anyway.
He sleeps a lot, my brother. Smiles in it. No sound.

I don't know. I never looked.

But he hums your songs. He keeps his right hand in his lap. And he's waited three hundred years for a bell that nobody rings. Whoever he was up there, someone must have loved him once. Nobody waits that long for nothing.

It's gone quiet all the way down. Not the Court. All of it. The whole Hollow stopped humming for a breath, the way you do when someone leaves the room.

Who was he?

...No. Don't tell me yet. Tell me some other time, when I'm older. I'd like there to be something left to find out.
